- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest. | How this version avoids them: PayHOA: we build no dues product and do not compete at about $2 per household. We price per association and per sale, and PayHOA is a setup option we recommend, so it is a partner rather than a rival. Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC: they serve incorporated associations with managers, whereas we create the legal counterparty they cannot. DIY templates and local attorneys (Nolo, LegalZoom-style forms): a template gives no notice, vote, proxy, minutes or recording service, and the attorney is our channel and supervising counsel rather than a substitute, because we take the work they cannot bill profitably. Maine statute: we productize it and plug its missing lien with the recorded covenant. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand signal, and our 'pre-formed association with a named contact' is exactly what such programs require. Local road-association managers and bookkeepers (unidentified): they sell ongoing bookkeeping, not closing-triggered formation, and could be subcontractors for annual administration.

title: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data
one_liner: An audit that tells research buyers what share of their online-panel responses came from bots, agents or fraud farms, and recalibrates the study against a verified-human control sample.
customer: Insights heads at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms, UX-research teams, academic labs and pollsters who buy panel sample from third-party vendors at $5-500 per complete.
problem: One prompt to a commercial AI agent now passes screeners and attention checks. A controlled evaluation found synthetic respondents passing 99.8% of 6,000 attention-check trials. As little as 3-7% contaminated responses can invalidate conclusions. Panel vendors both sell the sample and score its quality, so buyers cannot trust the referee.
solution: A per-study data-quality audit. Response files (timings, paradata, device data, open-ends) go through a detection ensemble plus honeypot items. A subset of the same questionnaire goes to a small address-recruited, device-attested human panel as a ground-truth control. Deliver an audit stamp, contamination-adjusted estimates, and a vendor scorecard across suppliers.
why_now: Survey-fraud research in 2025-26 shows agents beating attention checks. An MIT-run $50K challenge is testing detection, and NORC published a fraud literature review. Election-season polling and pharma sample budgets raise the stakes, and buyers are asking who audits the panels.
revenue_model: $3-15k per study audit, $50-150k per year programmes for insights teams that spend $2-10M on sample, and vendor-scorecard subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Most anti-fraud tooling is sold by panel sellers, whose incentive is to under-report fraud. The scarce asset is not detection code but an independent, verified-human comparison group, because you cannot prove what is fake without a known-real reference.
first_30_days: Recruit about 2,000 verified humans by address-based mail or a university survey-centre partnership. Buy sample from six panel vendors yourself and publish a 'state of sample quality' benchmark. Offer free audits to five insights leaders who have posted about bad data.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight.

title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.
lineage: mutation of I0428 ('Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte's Demand Package Review is carrier-side workflow (nurse review, 3-10 days, no LOP framing, no signature, no testimony). This is counsel-facing work product, signed and testifiable, and Enlyte reviewers can refer files to us for the signature layer instead of us fighting them for carriers. FAIR Health is a data input and the plaintiff expert's favorite anchor, so the kit pre-rebuts it instead of selling benchmarks. EvenUp is plaintiff-only and its demand packages become our intake format. Turquoise and CLARA sell rate analytics or claims software, not signed opinions. JurisPro-style billing experts are bespoke at $3-5k and slow. We take the repeatable 80% at a tenth of the price and hand the firm an expert only when a file justifies it. Starting in Georgia and Texas avoids Florida's statutory benchmark, and using payer and Medicare anchors avoids the weak hospital-file why-now.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Franchisee Flight Recorder and Recommendation Index
one_liner: Invert the advisor into a witness: a silent, tamper-evident ledger that records what the franchisor's AI recommended, what the owner ordered and what was binned, prices the gap under the owner's own contract, and scales into a franchisee-owned registry and a published Recommendation Cost Index for each chain.
customer: Start with legacy-contract Seven-Eleven owners in Kansai who fear OFC retaliation and will not use a tool that changes how they order. Then a franchisee-owned business cooperative, franchise-specialist law firms, lenders and analysts as data buyers, then regulators and convenience-store review panels as consumers of the aggregate. Later, Lawson and FamilyMart, Korea and Taiwan convenience chains, and other franchise systems with mandated promos, ordering or capex.
problem: The parent's insight stands: HQ recommendations optimize HQ's payoff. But advice tools stall on the owner's fear of the OFC, on HQ markdown pushes that commoditize the advice, and on Seven's new contract that shrinks the gap for new stores. Meanwhile owners have no evidence in the moments that matter: renewal or non-renewal talks, disputes about mismanagement, store sales, and any complaint to the JFTC or a METI panel. HQ holds the only record of what its AI recommended. The 2009 JFTC order on Seven-Eleven Japan and the Diamond and Toyo Keizai reporting show that regulators and press act on documented owner constraints, but individual owners hold anecdotes and one store is not statistics.
solution: Owner does nothing differently. Each day a LINE bot takes 3 photos or a forwarded CSV (the HQ order proposal screen, the order as placed, the disposal scan), extracts the data, and writes hashed records to a certified third-party time-stamp so the log is tamper-evident. The owner sees only a private monthly Ledger Statement: 'following HQ's proposals cost you X yen versus the optimum under your contract this month, Y yen cumulative', with no instruction and no OFC-visible change. The ledger is exported only on the owner's command to a lawyer, accountant, buyer or bank. Owners join a franchisee cooperative whose dues also fund a group-rate franchise-law retainer. Aggregated and anonymized across stores, the ledger yields per-item demand models that improve with store count and a quarterly Recommendation Cost Index for each chain, published as a neutral registry that regulators, lenders and press can cite. Every contract change (such as the 2027 Seven terms) becomes a natural experiment the index measures.
why_now: HQ AI ordering became the default at all three chains between 2023 and 2026, so a recorded 'recommended versus ordered versus binned' history now exists to capture. The disposal-share change in Seven's June 2026 contract shows HQ has conceded the conflict, and the METI convenience-store review panel is active. The 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka makes every wasted yen hurt more. Photo OCR and structured extraction make daily capture cost pennies, and certified time-stamping is standard infrastructure. The outcome of the 2023 union case (loss at the Supreme Court) shows that collective action needs a data and legal structure other than a labor union, which a cooperative can supply.
revenue_model: 1,980 yen per store per month from owners (about the price of consumer legal-expense insurance, an assumption to verify), with the cooperative dues bundled. Case packs for law firms at 300,000 to 500,000 yen with an expert declaration, optionally a contingency share where the law firm agrees. Annual data licenses to lenders, analysts and research bodies (roughly 3M to 10M yen each). At 15% of about 55,000 stores subscribing that is roughly 200M yen a year from owners alone, before case packs, licenses and other chains or countries. The registry and index are the longer-term standard-setting asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fear that blocks the advice product is the buying reason for the recorder. An owner who will never argue with the OFC will still pay a small fee for a private ledger he never has to show. The value is a network good: one owner's log is an anecdote, but thousands of timestamped logs are the only regulator-grade evidence that a franchisor's recommendations systematically diverge from franchisee payoff, and they cannot be replicated by anyone who lacks owner trust. Because it gives no advice it does not compete with HQ AI on accuracy and is immune to markdown-push commoditization, and it stays useful under any contract terms, including the 50/50 one where a gap remains (owner critical ratio about 36% versus HQ's about 70%).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the LINE bot and ledger on the founder's three stores (the first real evidence file) and commission a one-week franchise-lawyer memo on data ownership and confidentiality plus the business-cooperative structure. Days 10-30: pre-sell 30 owners at 1,980 yen per month for 12 months via Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups and 2 franchise-focused law firms, pitching it as 'a private record you never have to show anyone unless you need it'. Get one law firm to agree to a case-pack pilot price. Kill signals: fewer than 10 of 30 pre-sales, or the lawyer memo finds the HQ proposal screen cannot be recorded. Publish a one-page description of the Ledger Statement format and the planned index method to seed owner-to-owner sharing.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: It gives no ordering or markdown advice, so it does not compete with Seven, Lawson or FamilyMart AI, with Seven's markdown push, or with Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine, all of which are operational tools sold to retailers that inherit the retailer's payoff. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice and community but no evidence base or data, so they become referral channels and cooperative allies. HQ tools are the subject being recorded, and they cannot copy an independent record of their own recommendations without undermining themselves. Power sources: network economies in the pooled index, a cornered resource in owner-contributed logs, switching costs in years of timestamped history.

title: Satellite Witness for Neighbor Construction Claims
one_liner: A fixed-price, court-ready satellite-radar history of a condo tower's movement before and during the neighbor's pile-driving, sold through the plaintiff-side attorneys who represent Miami-Dade condo associations.
customer: Plaintiff-side construction and property-damage attorneys (start with about 25 Miami-Dade firms) who represent condo associations. The wedge buildings are barrier-island and downtown towers of 15+ stories in Sunny Isles Beach, Bal Harbour, Surfside, Edgewater, Brickell and Miami Beach that sit within roughly 200-300 m of permitted deep-foundation, dewatering or excavation work. The association's engineer and manager are co-users. Direct sales to boards come later.
problem: When a developer starts driving piles or dewatering next door, unit owners report cracks and vibration. The only pre-condition evidence is usually the developer's own visual crack survey, which is commissioned, held and dated by the party who may be liable. A sensor installed after work starts (SmartCore, about $20K at Marenas) has no baseline. A bespoke InSAR expert report from TRE or Fugro costs tens of thousands and takes months. The 2024 UM study found subsidence in 35 towers and tied some of it to nearby construction, so the fight is about causation: was the tower already sinking on fill, or did the neighbor's work do it? Without an independent baseline, associations either lose that argument or never file. This is a problem with a live trigger, a live adversary and a budget. It is not diligence the board has to be talked into.
solution: A permit-triggered evidence engine. (1) Monitor building, dewatering and foundation permits across Miami-Dade jurisdictions and auto-draw a 200-300 m influence zone around each site. (2) Process free Sentinel-1, OPERA DISP-S1 and ESA archive data into a retroactive per-building time series, so the baseline can be built after work has started. (3) Sell a $3,500 Causation Baseline Report: pre-construction trend, differential tilt across the footprint, and a difference-in-differences comparison against control towers on similar fill outside the zone. It ships with a hashed data package and a reproducible method note. (4) Sell $1,500/quarter Construction Watch, with a change memo each quarter. NISAR L-band corroborates it from June 2026 onward. (5) Provide a declaration and testimony through a contracted independent PE or geodesist, billed as pass-through. Everything is worded as a measurement of motion, never as a structural safety opinion. Work is structured as attorney-retained consulting.
why_now: The Dec 2024 UM/UH/GFZ study put construction-linked subsidence in Miami towers on the public record. Estructura's June 2026 Surfside-anniversary push has normalized InSAR for condos. Post-Surfside associations are hyper-vigilant and litigious. Florida courts apply the Daubert standard (since 2019), so a peer-reviewable, reproducible method matters. OPERA DISP-S1 (free since May 2025) and NISAR (public July 20, 2026) cut processing cost to near zero, while the expert-report incumbents still price as quote-based consulting. The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines have boards hiring engineers who now ask about neighbors.
revenue_model: Per engaged association: $3,500 baseline, plus $1,500/quarter Construction Watch averaging 8 quarters, plus expert pass-through at cost plus 20%. That is roughly $16K in the first 24 months at about 80% gross margin before expert time. A $299/month Permit Radar alert feed for firms and property managers covers their client lists. Attorneys often advance evidence costs on contingency or hybrid matters and recover them in settlement, so the law firm is often the effective payer. Target is about 40 engaged associations in year one, or about $600K revenue, then repeat cases per firm (3-5 a year). Later, the same engine feeds the wholesale-to-engineers layer from the parent idea.
non_obvious_insight: The satellite is a disinterested witness that logged the building before anyone had a dispute. That means the baseline is built retroactively, at the moment of peak willingness to pay, which sensors physically cannot do. The parent's 'no moat, open-source' weakness becomes a strength here: in a Daubert setting the opposing expert can re-run the method, so credibility comes from reproducibility, chain of custody, the control-tower design and a growing record of accepted declarations. The buyer is not buying monitoring, which boards avoid. They are buying leverage: a $3.5K report that turns a multi-million-dollar claim from unprovable to provable. Attorney-retained work also blunts the parent's 'discoverable bad report' problem, since the client chooses whether to disclose (confirm with counsel).
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the roughly 50 active or pending foundation, pile and dewatering permits in Sunny Isles, Edgewater, Brickell, Miami Beach, Surfside and Bal Harbour. Compute influence zones (about 700 towers) and run the free Sentinel-1/OPERA stack. Week 2: contract one university-affiliated geodesist or PE as expert of record. Cold-contact 25 plaintiff-side construction and condo firms and 10 property managers with a named sample: 'the six towers next to [site] have moved X mm/yr since 2016, and here is the control comparison.' Weeks 3-4: sell 3 design-partner baselines at $1,500, convert 2 to Construction Watch, and get one attorney to write a methodology-review letter. Kill test: if fewer than 3 of 25 firms take a paid pilot, or the expert will not put a name to the method, stop.
lineage: mutation of I1289 ('Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price. | How this version avoids them: Estructura and SmartCore sell forward-looking monitoring subscriptions to boards, built on sensors that cannot go back in time. This sells backward-looking, litigation-grade evidence through attorneys, triggered by a public permit event. TRE Altamira, Fugro, SkyGeo and NHAZCA sell bespoke quote-based expert projects at tens of thousands of dollars. This is a fixed $3,500 package with a pre-built method and a testifying expert on call. Sixense sells to contractors, who are the defendant side, so it is structurally conflicted here. OPERA is free but coarse and carries no chain of custody or expert. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo have no physical-movement data. SatSense and Detektia are not in Florida litigation workflows. The defensible pieces are the permit-lead engine, attorney relationships, an accepted-expert track record and the control-tower dataset.

title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.
lineage: mutation of I0195 ('Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building. | How this version avoids them: Ramco's warranty module is software that large operators run themselves, and I could not verify its claims. This is an outsourced, success-fee claims service for smaller buyers, which Ramco does not offer. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, though that is weak evidence. Generalist AP recovery-audit firms exist (an unresearched risk to check). They run duplicate-payment and vendor-statement logic and cannot read repair invoices, match serial numbers or judge warranty eligibility. Targeting pools and stations sidesteps PBH shielding, sidesteps the maintenance-system integration problem, and reduces relationship fear.

title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats.

title: Section-Level Hydrogen and Helium Leads for Landmen
one_liner: Sell 90-day exclusive, page-linked lists of Nemaha-corridor sections with hydrogen or helium evidence buried in old mud logs, DST reports and driller notes, to the landmen and lease shops who spend the first dollars of every junior's program.
customer: Independent landmen and lease-brokerage shops (2-50 people) in Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma who assemble acreage for natural hydrogen and helium juniors, plus the roughly 40-120 junior explorers themselves (Rystad counts 40, AKAP counts 123 companies). Wedge buyer: the lease shop, because it is paid per acre leased, has a hard deadline (leases are taken in a rush after each well announcement), and has no geoscientist on staff.
problem: The free datasets (USGS/BLM 16,000 gas analyses, KGS OFR 2025-59, SMU/GDR temperatures) already give away the structured layers, so an atlas built on them is worthless. What they omit is the unstructured evidence in page images at KCC/KGS-type archives: mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test gas notes, driller remarks such as 'gas would not burn', 'non-flammable' or 'heavy N2 odor', and water-well gas notes. Landmen today pick where to lease by copying the footprint of the last press release, which means they arrive after the price of a lease has already moved. Juniors that do this in-house (HyTerra, MAX Power, Koloma) are not customers, so the sellable market is the long tail and the lease shops serving it.
solution: A curated evidence-card product for one live fairway (Nemaha Uplift and Midcontinent Rift, KS/NE/OK). A VLM pipeline reads page images for a defined set of document types, a geologist verifies every card that reaches a customer, and each card carries the page image, the quoted text, and a confidence grade for sampling method, air-contamination signs (N2/O2 ratio) and analytical era. Cards roll up to a ranked list of 30-60 sections per block, plus a short 'do not lease' list of sections with clean hydrocarbon gas and no signal, which saves buyers money. Free layers (USGS, KGS, BLM/state mineral ownership) are ingested as baseline and shown for context but never sold. Delivered as a GeoPackage/KMZ and a PDF, with a courtroom-simple audit trail so a landman can defend the pick to a junior's board. Geothermal is dropped from v1 because SMU/GDR and GeoMap give it away.
why_now: Natural hydrogen went from about 10 to 40+ searching companies since 2020 (Rystad) and 123 by AKAP's count; HyTerra's Kansas McCoy 1 result (up to 83-96% H2) turned the Nemaha corridor into an active lease play in 2025-26, so lease shops need defensible picks right now. VLMs now read typed and handwritten well forms at cents per page, which broke the cost barrier that made a section-level re-read uneconomic before 2024. State surveys (KGS/KCC) are releasing more scans, and the academic OCR/LLM methods are public, which lowers the technical risk for a two-person team while making curation and speed the real product.
revenue_model: Entry pack: $5k non-exclusive, 3-township block. Exclusive block: $12-20k for a 90-day first-look on a 6-10 township block, renewable. Success fee: a capped per-net-acre finder fee (for example $2-5) or 0.5% ORRI on leases taken from exclusive-block sections. Year-1 bottom-up: 25 entry packs ($125k) + 6 exclusive blocks ($90k) + fees (~$50k) is about $265k with a two-person team; the business scales by adding fairways (Michigan/Ohio Rift extension, Colorado, Texas Panhandle helium) rather than by raising price per corridor. The buyer's ROI check: a 20,000-acre lease program at even $20-50/acre bonus is $0.4-1M, so a $5-15k pack is single-digit percent of spend.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not data, it is time-boxed scarcity. Lease information is perishable: once one buyer signs, the price of that section moves, so the value of a lead decays over weeks, and the right pricing unit is a 90-day exclusive option on a block, exactly how prospect generators sell in oil and gas. Second, the 0.5% hit rate seen in the Paris Basin OCR study (26 wells of about 5,000) is a weakness for a broad atlas but a strength for a precision shortlist: sell 40 sections, not 40,000, and let the 'do not lease' list carry the rest of the value. Third, buyers who drill a lead and share the result get a discount, and those results become a private ground-truth set that calibrates the confidence score, which no free dataset can copy.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick the Nemaha corridor counties in Kansas, download KGS/KCC scanned ACO-1 forms, driller logs, DST reports and mud logs for about 5,000 wells, and run VLM extraction on the four document types. Week 2: have a geologist verify the top 150 candidate cards and produce a 60-section block map with page-image links. Week 3: contact 10 lease shops and 10 juniors (LinkedIn plus the AAPL and Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association member lists) with one free sample card and a demo map. Week 4: ask for a $5k prepay for the block pack. Kill test from the parent: if fewer than 3 of 10 prepay, stop and go to the state-survey channel instead. Also offer an exclusive 90-day option on the sections buyers like best.
lineage: mutation of I1085 ('Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side. | How this version avoids them: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR, GeoMap and EPRI: we sell only what they omit (unstructured page-level evidence and curated section lists) and use them free as baseline, so a free download cannot replace the product. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: they hold their own in-house archives and are not customers, and our buyers are the lease shops and the long tail they cannot serve. NthDS and Enverus/TGS: they sell per-well files ($70-80 LAS) to O&G buyers and have no hydrogen or helium curation; they are more likely acquirer or data partner than rival, and our per-section conclusion with a human-verified audit trail is a different unit. Heologic, AKAP, Wood Mackenzie, Rystad: they sell company- or project-level intelligence or soil-gas anomalies, not lease-block, page-linked evidence. Terra AI and HyReveal model, but lack the extracted page-level inputs. Geothermal (Zanskar, GeoMap, SMU/GDR) is deliberately excluded.

title: Pet Claims Clearinghouse Starting at the Front Desk
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of insurers policing vet invoices after the fact, give vet clinics a carrier-agnostic estimate-to-payout tool at the counter, then grow it into the standard transaction layer for pet insurance and a same-day payment network.
customer: Practice managers and lead client-service staff at independent and small-group US general-practice clinics (2-8 vets), and emergency or specialty hospitals where tickets run above $1,500. There are about 28,000 US vet hospitals. Later payers are pet insurers (per clean claim) and financing partners (per referred loan).
problem: An owner stands at the counter with a $3,800 estimate and says 'I have insurance'. It is one of about 15 carriers, the front desk cannot tell what will be covered, and the owner declines, delays, goes on credit or, in the worst case, euthanizes. Survey data shows 85% of vet professionals see owners decline recommended care at $1,000 or less, and they estimate about 13% of euthanasia decisions are driven by cost. After treatment, staff spend up to 30 minutes per claim in each insurer's own portal. Trupanion's VetDirect Pay shows clinics adopt this when it removes paperwork and lets them quote net of insurance (about 11,500 clinics as of October 2025, and a Digitail integration in August 2026), but it works only for Trupanion pets. Trupanion holds roughly 12% share in the market estimates found, so most insured pets have no such tool.
solution: Wedge product (shippable in about 10 weeks). Estimate Check: the front desk uploads the estimate or PMS export and the owner's policy PDF or insurance card. The tool returns per-line 'likely covered, likely excluded, needs records', a projected reimbursement range, and a one-page owner sheet showing what they will likely pay today and after reimbursement, with a financing option for any gap. It also shows the parent's edit logic turned around as provider-side scrubber tips ('these five lines are usually treated as included in the surgical fee; quote as a package price'). Claim Pack: after treatment it assembles the canonical invoice, records and the insurer's form, sends it through that insurer's intake channel, and tracks status. Network path: every estimate and reimbursement outcome trains per-insurer payout predictions. A published open transaction set (estimate, eligibility, claim, remittance on VeNom-based codes) is offered to insurers, who adopt it to cut intake cost. Later, an instant advance to clinics on insurer remits, funded by a warehouse line, turns it into a balance-sheet payment network.
why_now: Direct-pay proved clinic demand, but it is fragmented by carrier: Digitail and Trupanion announced their integration only in August 2026, and each new PMS-insurer pair is a one-off build. Insured pets are growing about 9% a year on a 4.27% penetration base, so the share of clinic estimates touched by insurance keeps rising. LLMs can now read arbitrary policy PDFs and messy estimates, which is what previously made a multi-carrier tool uneconomic. Corporate consolidation and price inflation make estimate conversations harder every quarter.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $199 a month per clinic location, sold on saved staff hours and higher treatment-plan acceptance, with a first-month free trial. Phase 2: insurers pay $0.75-$1.50 per clean canonical claim (their manual intake cost, an assumption to test), and financing partners pay a referral fee on loans originated at the estimate moment. Phase 3: 1.5-2.5% on advanced remit dollars (assumed range). Illustrative year-5 scale: 3,000 clinics at $2.4k is about $7M, 5M claims at $1 is about $5M, and $1B of advanced remits at 2% is about $20M, so roughly $30M of revenue on about a quarter of an estimated $4B of US claims paid.
non_obvious_insight: In human health, most claim edits run on the provider side, in clearinghouse scrubbers, before submission. Edits create value when they change behavior before the service, not when they reduce a payment afterwards. In pet insurance the only party who can renegotiate an estimate is the vet at the counter, and the only party with a real incentive at that moment is the clinic, because declined treatment is lost revenue. Flipping the parent's edits to the provider side removes its central risk (balance bills without vet contracts) and makes the vet a voluntary distribution channel. Whoever owns the estimate screen owns the transaction standard, just as the claim form did in human health, and the standard is worth more than any single edit library.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: recruit an ex-practice-manager co-founder and sit with 10 clinics, shadowing 30 insured-estimate conversations. Collect 200 real estimates with matching policy documents and reimbursement outcomes from 5 friendly clinics. Week 2-3: build the line normalizer and coverage rules for the top 8 carriers from public policy forms. Week 3-4: run a manual-assist 'Estimate Check in 15 minutes' service for 10 clinics by text or email, free, and score predictions against actual reimbursements (target: within 10% of the actual payout on at least 70% of cases). Convert 5 clinics to $199 a month by day 30 and ask the two most engaged to introduce their PMS account manager, which starts the marketplace-app conversation.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.
