- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are producer-side herd management or tracking tools, and none holds lender pledge data. They cannot collect it without alienating the producers who pay them. Merck/Allflex and Vence own tags but a vendor-run registry would be distrusted by rival tag vendors and lenders. IMI Global's Beef Passport ties EIDs to verification records for the supply chain, not to liens or exits. State central-filing systems and brand agencies are passive, annual or paper-based lists, so we sit on top of them and can partner. The real risks are sale-barn clerking-software vendors and state agencies adding matching. Being lender-funded and neutral, with lender pledge data as the cornered resource, is the counter.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CBP e-Recordation and free CBP/IPR Center resources (DIY substitute), Corsearch (Brand Protection), Red Points, OpSec Security / Crane Authentication. White space: Confidence caveat: every WebSearch call was refused because the session's 200-search budget was already spent, so this verdict rests on about 35 direct WebFetch pulls plus prior knowledge. I found no funded startup or incumbent selling a done-for-you, small-brand, monitored CBP program (recordation, ID guide, 24-hour authentication desk, detention monitoring, evidence packaging). That is weaker evidence than a clean search sweep, so rerun searches for customs recordation subscription services, and for the CBP offerings of Red Points, Corsearch and IP boutiques, before building. What looks unserved: (1) Enterprise vendors (Corsearch, CSC, OpSec/Crane, MarkMonitor) sell online takedowns to large brands and none of their homepages mention customs; sub-$30M brands are not their customer. (2) Law firms treat recordation as a one-off filing, not a monitored program with an authentication desk; CBP asks for responses within 24 hours (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/priority-issues/ipr/bestpractices), so speed of response is the real product and it is an operations business. (3) Nobody found connects marketplace lookalike listings to bill-of-lading importers for small brands. Skeptical flags, most severe first: (1) Fee-sharing and unauthorized practice of law: a non-lawyer company taking 20-30% of settlements and receiving referral fees from IP counsel likely conflicts with ABA Model Rule 5.4-style bans on splitting fees with non-lawyers in most US states; get a legal opinion before fixing pricing. (2) CBP acts on counterfeit marks and recorded copyrights, not on look-alike dupes or trade-dress copies, so many indie-brand clones (copied design, no logo) are out of reach and the addressable pain is smaller than the pitch implies. (3) Importer identity: before seizure CBP typically does not give the trademark owner the importer name and address; unredacted images or samples come only after the importer gets notice and 7 business days to respond, and full importation details including importer name and address follow seizure within 30 business days (19 CFR 133.21, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.21). BOL matching is the workaround, but public BOL data covers mostly ocean cargo, importers can request confidentiality (from memory, unverified), and much knockoff volume moves as parcels or via forwarders and non-resident importers. (4) Recordation needs a USPTO registration (about $350 per class) or a registered copyright, and many $1-30M brands lack full coverage. (5) The lever is $190 per class and the recordation, ID guide and training routes are free on cbp.gov, so the subscription must sell speed, labor and outcomes, not access. (6) Lever-rule (19 CFR 133.23, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.23) covers gray-market goods that are physically and materially different; it does not address knockoffs and is a niche add-on.

title: Stability Mark: Verified-Stable Tower Registry
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of screening buildings for sinking, certify the many towers that have been stable for 10-30 years with a satellite-verified public mark and lookup registry that agents, lenders and insurers can trust, later backed by a scoping guarantee.
customer: Wedge: boards and building-specialist listing agents at older concrete towers (1970s-2000s) in Aventura, Sunny Isles, Bal Harbour, Brickell and Miami Beach whose owners are stuck with post-Surfside price discounts and need to prove soundness. Second wave: lenders, title companies, master-policy underwriters and MLS platforms as registry API subscribers. Engineers act as co-signers and reviewers.
problem: After Surfside, buyers, lenders and insurers treat every older tower as suspect until proven otherwise. Milestone and SIRS reports are long, alarming to non-engineers and describe conditions, not movement. Florida condo scores like Domexa's or CondoScan's rest on paperwork (did the board file on time?), not on how the ground and structure have behaved. Fine buildings cannot prove they are fine, and unit owners eat a discount. The parent idea also has a demand flaw: boards do not buy reports that might create a discoverable bad document. Selling fear to a reluctant buyer is hard.
solution: The Stability Mark: a 1-page certificate with a QR code to a live registry page, issued only to towers that pass published, pre-registered criteria. Example criteria: at least 10 years of persistent-scatterer coverage (Sentinel-1 alone gives 2016-2026; ERS/Envisat extend it if Miami coverage is usable), no differential settlement above a stated threshold, no accelerating trend, and a matched-control comparison. Participation is opt-in. Passing towers are published. Ambiguous or failing towers get a private result and a monitoring plan, with no public listing. The certificate covers the measurement, not structural safety, and a PE co-signs the method. The method is open and reproducible. There is annual re-verification with automatic revocation triggers, MLS-compatible listing fields, and a lender and insurer API. In year two, add a Scoping Guarantee: a reinsured parametric cover that pays for the Phase 1 engineering evaluation ($15-40K) if a certified tower later trips the threshold, priced at about $150/building/year. The certifier's own capital then stands behind the mark.
why_now: Post-Surfside stigma on older Florida towers is still discounting resale values, and inventory has been elevated since 2024-25 (verify current data). The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines are about to push a wave of alarming paperwork at buyers who cannot interpret it. Reserves can no longer be waived from 2026, so buyers ask about condition. Only satellite archives hold a 1990s-to-present record of how a tower behaved: FIU found Champlain Towers South's 1990s subsidence in ERS data, and no sensor bought today can create that history. Free Sentinel-1 and OPERA data plus NISAR (L-band, from June 2026) make re-verification cheap. Estructura's fear-first marketing leaves the good-news position empty.
revenue_model: Initial certificate $1,800 per building ($995 founding price for the first 50), then $500/year re-verification. PE review fee of about $250 per certificate, and about $60-100 of compute per building. Year two: registry API for lenders, title and insurers at $20K/year flat or $1-3 per lookup, and Scoping Guarantee premium of about $150 per building per year. Year one: about 150 marks at about $1,400 average is roughly $210K, plus $75K recurring. The 10x case: several thousand concrete towers in Florida and tens of thousands nationwide (assumed, verify), with Gulf, Houston, Tampa, Jersey City and Honolulu next. A registry adopted by MLS platforms and lenders, plus a warranty book, is a platform business that a report shop cannot become.
non_obvious_insight: Mandatory-inspection regimes create fear purchases. A voluntary mark creates status purchases, and it has an unraveling dynamic: once 20-30% of comparable towers in a submarket carry the mark, silence becomes a signal that a building is sinking or hiding something, so competitors' badges drive demand rather than the board's fear. Demand rises non-linearly with adoption, which no report business gets. The 10-30 year archive is a cornered resource: nobody can retroactively install a 1996 sensor. Every engineer-reviewed pass or fail adds to a proprietary labeled dataset of which radar signatures precede real findings, which tightens the thresholds and beats sensor bundles that only see the future. The warranty forces honest calibration, since the certifier pays if it is wrong.
first_30_days: Take the parent's roughly 400-tower Sentinel-1 stack and process the 150 oldest concrete towers against the full available archive. Publish the pass criteria before running the results. Confirm persistent-scatterer density and ERS/Envisat usability on Miami; if pre-2015 coverage is poor, use the Sentinel-1 decade. Contract one PE or geodesist to co-sign a methodology memo with measurement-only wording. Approach 10 building-specialist listing agents and 10 presidents of towers that passed, at the $995 founding price. Aim for 8 marks sold, 3 live on agent sites or MLS remarks with the QR code, and 2 lenders or title underwriters willing to read the registry page. Kill test: if fewer than 5 of 20 boards buy at $995, or no PE will co-sign the wording, stop.
lineage: mutation of I1289 ('Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price. | How this version avoids them: Estructura, SmartCore, TRE Altamira, Fugro, Sixense and the other InSAR shops all sell risk detection and monitoring, which is a fear purchase, and none offers a public verified-stable credential. Estructura is also counter-positioned against it: its sensor and AI subscription depends on unseen risk, and a satellite all-clear would cannibalize it, so it cannot rationally copy the mark. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo are paperwork-based scores, paid by buyers at thin price points ($49). The Stability Mark supplies the physical-behavior layer they lack, so Domexa is a distribution partner (they could embed the mark in their scores). OPERA is free but coarse and carries no attestation or per-building certificate. SatSense and Detektia target insurers and engineers abroad. The moat is a published standard, a PE panel, MLS and lender adoption, a labeled dataset and guarantee capital. A copycat has to rebuild all of it.

title: Phantom-Load Registry: Land Records Meet Utility Queues
one_liner: A utility-funded vetting desk that joins courthouse land-assembly signals with co-op and municipal large-load inquiry logs, so it can say which 100-1,000 MW projects are real and which LLC families are shopping the same megawatts to five utilities.
customer: Electric co-ops, G&Ts, municipal utilities and PUDs with 5-person engineering staffs. They pay per memo or on retainer. Secondary buyers are developers' land teams and site-selection consultants, infrastructure and energy funds buying alt-data, and county economic-development offices.
problem: Every party sees half the picture. A small utility sees the inquiry (an LLC, a MW ask, a PowerPoint) but not the land trail. The land-assembly watcher sees option memoranda and easements but cannot tell a real hyperscale campus from a speculator flipping dirt. Nobody sees the same MW shopped across states. Texas SB 6's collateral rule (final expected by end of 2026) will push phantom load onto softer neighbors.
solution: First product is the fixed-price vetting memo ($7.5-25k) with a red/amber/green result and a recommended security amount. The site-control and LLC-principal items in the 12-point physical-reality test are powered by an image-level read of recorded options, leases and easements, clustered by return-to law firm, notary, signatory and mailing address. Air-permit and equipment-slot checks come from the vetting desk. Utilities that share their inquiry logs (LLC, MW, node, date, outcome) get discounted memos. Those logs become a multi-utility duplicate-request registry that flags land-assembled-but-no-equipment-slot projects and the same LLC family filing at several utilities. Later products are a county-level real-versus-phantom alert feed and alt-data licenses for funds.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (PUCT rule final due by 12/31/2026, $50,000/MW security) is exporting speculators to neighboring states. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or cancelled, so utilities are burned and skeptical. FinCEN's 2025 exemption for domestic companies means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision now reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $7.5-25k per vetting memo. $60-150k per year G&T retainers. $2-8k per month regional developer seats. $750-2,000 per tract title packet. $50-150k per year alt-data licenses for funds. Utilities often pass memo cost to applicants as a study-deposit line item. Later, registry subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Land records show intent, and an option memo is cheap to buy. The equipment and permit trail shows capability. The utility queue shows the ask. No single dataset separates real from speculative, but the join does. Land assembled with no transformer slot, by an LLC family filing at five utilities, is a land flip. Each utility's eventual outcome (built, cancelled, withdrawn) is also a free labeled training set for the tape's classifier, which no scraper competitor can get. Utilities will only share inquiry logs with someone they already trust to vet, and that is a trust position a pure data vendor lacks.
first_30_days: Through state electric cooperative associations, get 3 co-ops to hand over their last 10 inquiries each. Pull 24 months of recorded instruments in those territories, plus state air-permit and LLC filings. Run a free back-test showing which past inquiries were real. Publish a '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' one-pager and send a sample 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants. Convert 2-3 co-ops to paid $7.5k memos on live inquiries and pitch one G&T retainer.
lineage: hybrid of I0773 + I0079 (Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure + Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities). Why stronger: The vetting desk alone is a services business with a thin data moat, and the tape alone fights for alt-data budgets with no ground-truth labels. Together, memo revenue funds data collection, utility outcomes label the data, and the pooled duplicate registry gets more valuable with each utility that joins. ACV rises, and utilities can be reached through co-op associations instead of cold outreach.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Auto Add-On Refund Cascade: Payoff and Return Desk
one_liner: One refund engine for auto add-ons (GAP and service contracts) with two triggers, California's new 3-day return for dealers and the loan payoff for credit unions, sold through the lender who touches both.
customer: California credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and indirect-lending departments), who pay for payoff recovery and can introduce their dealer networks. California independent and buy-here-pay-here used-car dealers selling 30-200 cars a month, who pay per return. Later, MGAs and insurers buying return-risk data.
problem: Dealers with no back office must unwind a returned car (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales-tax reversal, commissions) inside a very short refund deadline, and fragmented dealers are expensive to reach. Credit unions leave unearned GAP and service-contract refunds unclaimed at payoff because consumer refund sites wait for borrowers to show up. Both jobs depend on knowing what roughly 60 administrators actually require and how fast they pay.
solution: A shared cancellation-cascade engine: administrator playbook and response-time data, a 50-state pro-rata rule set, and generated cancellation packets tracked to payment. Trigger A (dealers): forward the cancellation notice and the desk notifies the lender, submits administrator cancellations, prepares DMV and tax reversals, calculates refund and permitted deductions, and stores the compliance file, at $195-250 per return or a $99 per month standby plan. Trigger B (lenders): free retrospective audit of 500 past payoffs, then $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered refunds. Pitch the credit union as the channel: 'Your dealers' returns start hitting your payoff desk October 1. We give your dealer network a standby unwind plan, and your members automatic refunds.'
why_now: California's SB 766 takes effect Oct 1, 2026, two days from today, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has run a mandatory used-car return at this scale. Roughly 3M repossessions a year, 84-month loans and about 30% of trade-ins underwater mean many loans die early with stacked add-ons, and buyers who suddenly cannot afford the payment are the likeliest to return. LLMs can now read messy contract images cheaply.
revenue_model: Per-return fee of $195-250 and $99 per month per-store standby retainer. Credit union payoff fee of $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered money. Attorney deficiency audits at $99 each. Phase 2: 10-20% of premium as MGA on a $60-120 per used unit return-risk cover. Phase 3: license the cascade workflow to dealer management systems and eContract vendors, and sell administrator refund-speed benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: These are one business with two triggers. Every California return teaches the desk how each administrator behaves (what they demand, how fast they pay), which makes payoff-refund collections faster and more predictable, and every payoff audit produces the dollar totals that open lender doors. The credit union's indirect dealer network is the only cheap channel to hundreds of small dealers, and the lender is motivated because a dealer's botched unwind becomes the lender's compliance and funding headache. Return and payoff data together also price the return-risk insurance nobody can price today.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents with the $99 standby plan and a 24-hour turnaround promise. Pitch 3 California credit unions with indirect programs on a free 500-payoff retro audit plus a dealer-network standby offer. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a spreadsheet and e-sign, and log the time and dollar cost of every step.
lineage: hybrid of I0109 + I1151 (Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions + Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return). Why stronger: The lender relationship solves the return desk's distribution problem, and the return desk hands the payoff product a must-have, time-boxed reason to get a meeting. One administrator database serves both, so unit cost falls with volume and collection speed improves. The combined dataset is what makes the return-risk MGA product priceable, which neither parent can reach alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Recall Drills: State QC Findings Become Worker Training
one_liner: A recall-notice system for SNAP errors: every finding from a state's own QC review and every H.R.1 rule change becomes a dollar-tagged synthetic drill within 14 days, delivered through the state's CQI field staff to new hires in its highest-error counties, with an audit trail for corrective-action plans.
customer: Wedge: North Carolina's SNAP continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) unit. Its staff are former county workers who visit each of the 100 county departments monthly, plus the counties the state has already flagged as high-error. NC's 6.69% rate sits 0.69 points above the 6% cliff, and the parent research puts crossing it at about $140M a year. Payer: the state SNAP director's training/CQI line. Users: CQI specialists and county supervisors. Next states: Louisiana (7.61%) and any state within about 1.5 points of a 6/8/10% tier line.
problem: QC findings reach workers months after the case action, as webinars and memos. H.R.1 rule churn (work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance changes) creates fresh errors faster than classroom training absorbs them. New hires learn on live caseloads, and Kansas cites turnover as an error driver. Counties are told 'documenting, documenting, documenting' but have no per-worker evidence trail. A handful of CQI staff cannot be in 100 counties every day.
solution: Three pieces. (1) An error-to-drill pipeline: CQI staff upload a QC finding at element level (stacked shelter deduction after a rent change, biweekly pay-stub conversion, household member who left). Within 14 days we return a synthetic twin case, scored with PolicyEngine as the oracle and hand-checked against the state manual, and push it to the assigned counties. (2) A 30-day new-hire certification track over the top three error elements, with pre/post scores and time-to-competency. (3) A CQI console with per-county and per-worker error-type heatmaps and a one-click 'CAP evidence packet' PDF (assigned, completed, score trend) that counties attach to corrective-action documentation. Drills test the input and verification decisions workers actually make (what to verify, which income to budget, which old entry to close), not the arithmetic the eligibility system already does.
why_now: The FY2027 QC sample year opens Oct 1, 2026. It is the first year measured under the new rules and it sets the FY2030 cost share (FY2029 and later use the rate from three fiscal years earlier). FY2028 exposure is effectively locked to the state's better of FY2025 or FY2026, so the next lever is FY2027 onward. The 75% state/local admin cost share also starts Oct 1, 2026. USDA published FY2025 rates on June 24, 2026: 41 states are above 6% and the national rate is 10.62%, and states above 6% must file remediation plans. States are visibly buying: Alabama DHR posted a QC assessment and training RFP, and NC's one-click 'close old deduction' prompt has been used more than 20,000 times, which shows targeted micro-interventions get adopted.
revenue_model: Year-1 state pilot of $60-90k for 12-15 named counties (verify it sits under each state's small-purchase limit). This expands to statewide at $250-400k a year. Counties outside the state contract pay $150-300 per worker, and new-hire certification is $250 per hire. All prices are unvalidated, so get the budget line from the CQI director before writing case #13. Realistic ceiling is about $10-20M ARR across the roughly 40 states above the threshold, so this is the modest-ceiling, fast-to-cash version.
non_obvious_insight: The product is closing the lag, not teaching skill. States already hold the scarcest asset, their own QC findings, and lose months turning it into training. A recall loop (finding, twin drill, completion evidence) cannot be copied by a vendor that only has the generic USDA taxonomy. It is one data-sharing MOU with a state QC unit away, and US Digital Response reports such agreements take 3 weeks to 3 months. Pick the launch state by distance to a cliff times benefit dollars, not by pain: NY at 13% needs a 3-point cut just to reach the 10% tier, while NC at 6.69% can plausibly cross 6%. A 0%-error county is still charged for the state average, so the state CQI unit, not the county, is the customer.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls with NC CQI staff, county DSS directors and the state county association, asking who owns a budget line for this and what the last training tool cost. Days 5-15: build 12 drills from public sources only (H.R.1 rule changes, the publicly described stacked-shelter-deduction failure, biweekly wage conversion, household-member removal), and script the 14-day finding-to-drill workflow. Days 15-25: run a 3-county new-hire pre/post pilot with CQI staff as co-facilitators. Days 25-30: hand the state a CAP evidence packet sample and a one-page letter of intent with a price, and ask the CQI director to name the budget line.
lineage: mutation of I1240 ('Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget ran out before I could run any searches, so this is a partial check. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 URLs (the idea's cited sources, Maximus, PCG, PSI, Code for America, Kognito, Relias, Deloitte, Route Fifty) plus GitHub repo searches. Several sites returned 403, 404 or 503. It could not cover Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch, or find startup names. The absence of a found direct competitor is therefore weaker than a full search would give, and should be re-checked with searches such as 'SNAP eligibility worker training simulation', 'benefits caseworker AI roleplay startup', and 'eligibility training' RFPs before the founder commits.

What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). (3) New-hire ramp-up: Kansas cited turnover and caseworker training complexity as drivers of its errors, and no product measures time-to-competency.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats. | How this version avoids them: Maximus Accuracy Assistant flags risk inside the live workflow and does not train. We use the same error patterns upstream and can pass them to Maximus, so it is a channel or acquirer, not a rival. State academies and NC's monthly QC webinars are free supply, but they are lecture-style with no per-worker measurement. We arm the CQI staff who run them and produce evidence they cannot. Code for America and PolicyEngine are flow and rules tools. PolicyEngine is a commodity input to our scoring, and the moat is the state's own finding library plus the audit trail. Kognito sold soft-skill simulations with no dollar metric. Every drill here is tagged to a QC element and its cost-share exposure. PCG, PSI and Deloitte sell consultant hours, while this is a persistent loop and evidence record priced below a single consultant week.

title: Contributor-Only Delay Outcome Ledger for Immigration Solos
one_liner: A give-to-get ledger that joins public dockets with the USCIS action dates only the filing lawyer sees, sold as a triage score plus a consent-order-first filing pack for a solo's existing stuck files in the four highest-moot districts.
customer: Solo and 2-5 attorney immigration firms whose book is mostly naturalization, family-based, I-751 and I-765 work, already admitted in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. or E.D. Mich. (the districts where Mandamus.com's own tally shows 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action). Narrowest wedge: a firm holding 10+ files already past posted times or more than 120 days past a naturalization interview. Those are existing paying clients, so each filing is a $2.5-5k upsell with zero acquisition cost. Secondary buyers later: boutique mandamus firms and litigation funders, as data licensees.
problem: Solos sit on stuck files and do not file, for reasons the judges and the competitor research surfaced. (1) They cannot tell which suits will be quietly mooted and which will draw a motion to dismiss: nationality-hold suits went 0-13 in D.D.C. this summer, and the Fifth Circuit bars I-485 delay claims (Cheejati). (2) They cannot price a flat fee without knowing the tail if the government fights. (3) A free pro se guide plus a $5,000 boutique make a $400 drafting tool look redundant, and general AI drafting is eroding the 6-10 hour learning curve. Public stats are hand-tallied for about 7 districts, and a docket shows when a case ended, not why or when USCIS actually acted.
solution: Three pieces, all attorney-of-record signed (the company is software). (1) Stuck-Case Book: paste or CSV-import pending cases from any case-management export (no partnership needed). It ranks each file by ripeness and expected days from service to USCIS action. Ripeness is tiered: N-400s more than 120 days after interview under 8 U.S.C. 1447(b), where the statute supplies the clock and in most circuits USCIS cannot adjudicate until the court remands, come first; then I-751, I-765 and long-idle I-130/I-140 under the APA. It refuses to generate filings for nationality-hold and Fifth Circuit I-485 cases and says why. (2) Filing pack: complaint, exhibits, service checklist, 60-day answer calendar, a documented pre-suit exhaustion checklist (e-request, Ombudsman, congressional inquiry) that also builds the 'not substantially justified' record, and a consent-order-first settlement template with an express EAJA reservation and a 30-day fee-petition reminder. (3) The ledger: after each case the attorney logs service date, USCIS action date and how it ended (consent order, quiet adjudication, MTD granted or denied). Judge- and AUSA-level detail unlocks only for contributors; everyone else gets a free coarse district scorecard.
why_now: The Oct 2025 end of the 540-day EAD auto-extension made I-765 delay suits a primary remedy, and holds keep files idle, but D.D.C.'s June-Aug 2026 record (government 13-0) means undifferentiated 'just file' now loses, so triage suddenly has value it lacked two years ago. LLM drafting has turned complaint templates into a commodity, pushing value to judgment and data. Honest caveat: RECAP counts look flat (385, 352, 477 filings a year in 2023-25), so the pitch is a higher win rate per filing, not a volume surge.
revenue_model: Free: coarse district scorecard (lead magnet and SEO). Paid: $299/month Ledger Pro (unlimited Stuck-Case Book, 2 filing packs a month, judge/AUSA-level data for contributors), extra packs $250 each. Flat fees only, never a share of the lawyer's fee. Year 2: data licenses ($1-3k/month) to boutique firms, litigation funders and case-management vendors. Bottom-up (assumptions to validate): about 1,500 target solos in the four districts x 20% penetration x about $3.6k/year is roughly $1.1M ARR before adding districts.
non_obvious_insight: A docket records when a suit ended, not when or why USCIS acted; stipulations and the 60-day answer clock add weeks of noise. The real key is service date, then USCIS action date, then dismissal type, and only the filing lawyer holds the approval notice. Every competing stat (Mandamus.com's hand tally, Lex Machina/Trellis-style docket analytics, raw CourtListener) is blind to it, so the moat is a cornered resource that accrues only through contributors and cannot be scraped. Second, the solo's blocking question is not 'can I draft this' but 'what does it cost me if the government fights'; tail probability by district is what lets them quote a confident flat fee.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: run the 8 real web searches the prior research could not (mandamus AI, delay-suit software, Crunchbase, AILA toolkits). Days 1-21: hand-label roughly 300 USCIS delay dockets from 2023-26 in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. and E.D. Mich. from CourtListener/RECAP (cause of ending, days to end) and publish a free district scorecard. Days 7-30: pull the roughly 60 attorneys of record who file most of those suits (public) and offer free lifetime Founding Contributor status in exchange for backfilling 10 past cases with USCIS action dates from their approval notices; separately offer 100+ non-filing solos in the same districts a free 10-minute Stuck-Case Book audit of their own pending files and pre-sell 5 at $299/month. Go/no-go: 5 paying firms and 100+ outcomes with action dates logged by day 30.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com sells suits to consumers at $5,000 and has no lawyer-facing product; this targets its would-be referrers, treats it as a data buyer, and builds a joined dataset it cannot hand-tally. Docketwise has no litigation features; this rides on CSV export so it does not depend on it, and if Docketwise adds templates it still cannot copy a contributor-fed ledger. Lex Machina/Trellis and CourtListener see docket events only, not agency action dates or consent-versus-quiet outcomes; this builds on CourtListener rather than competing with it. DoNotPay and general AI drafting compete on drafting; this sells calibrated judgment (which suit, where, with what settlement structure) and refuses bad cases. Alma and Boundless are consumer or visa firms, not tools, and are potential customers.

title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SGS (independent inspection, sampling and assay), Bureau Veritas / Inspectorate (commodities inspection), Intertek (Caleb Brett / minerals and battery testing), Alex Stewart International. White space: Provisional, because the research was severely constrained: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any search ran, and the direct fetches of incumbent sites returned 403, 404 or no relevant content. Nothing below is web-verified. Likely unserved: (1) A sampling-variance-certified referee product, meaning a Gy/TOS-based protocol with a stated sampling variance, heterogeneity characterisation (variography, sampling nomogram) and a binding-settlement clause. Inspection majors sell 'independent sampling and assay' as a commodity service, but I found no evidence that they publish or guarantee sampling uncertainty for black mass. (2) On-site, containerised, inert-atmosphere sample prep at the recycler or gigafactory gate. Black mass is being pushed toward hazardous-waste treatment in the EU, which makes shipping bulk samples to distant labs harder. (3) Tying lot-level sampling data to EU Battery Regulation material-recovery and recycled-content documentation. The main risk is that SGS, Bureau Veritas/Inspectorate, Intertek or Alex Stewart already offer black-mass sampling and umpire assay and would call this an existing service. The whole wedge depends on their protocols being meaningfully worse than TOS practice, which is unproven and is exactly what the free duplicate-sampling study would test.

title: Day-Zero Payoff Bridge for Floorplan Dealers
one_liner: Invert the radar: instead of catching dealers who fail to pay the floorplan lender, wire the payoff directly to the lender the day the car sells and get repaid when the retail contract funds, turning sold-out-of-trust risk into a short, fully secured receivable with data-driven underwriting.
customer: Independent and franchised dealers that sell through third-party indirect finance and get squeezed when contracts in transit, stips or unwinds stretch funding beyond the floorplan payoff window. Pilot referral partners are two or three independent floorplan lenders. Capital comes from a credit fund or family-office vehicle buying short-dated receivables. Dealer pays a per-deal fee, and the floorplan lender shares in it and saves audit cost and risk.
problem: SOT often starts as a timing gap, not fraud. The dealer has delivered the car, the retail lender has not yet funded, and the floorplan payoff clock is running. That is why honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books for a week or more, and it is how a small cash squeeze becomes fraud. Detection tools (including the parent) only tell the lender after the timing gap has already turned into a loss or a phone call. Floorplan lenders then hold reserves and audit constantly because they cannot see the cash in transit.
solution: When a floored car sells, the dealer requests a bridge with the payoff quote, bill of sale and contract or funding-approval docs (LLM-parsed). We verify the sale with the listing signal (retail-sale signature) and cross-check the payoff quote, then wire the payoff directly to the floorplan lender, so cash never touches the dealer and cannot be diverted. We are repaid when the retail lender funds the contract, through a lockbox or deposit-account control agreement, or a notice of assignment where the retail lender allows it. The risk is receivable dilution (an unwound or charged-back contract from a creditworthy obligor), not dealer fraud. Underwriting uses obligor identity, the dealer's payoff-lag history, the dealer's unwind and chargeback record, and the listing check. Rollout runs in three phases. (1) A free dealer-side 'Unpaid VIN clock' built on the radar signal is the top of funnel and lets aged sold-not-paid VINs self-select. (2) A capped concierge bridge of up to $25k per unit. (3) Floorplan lenders name Day-Zero as an approved payoff method, in return for lower reserves and audit frequency, and receivables are sold forward to credit funds so the startup stays capital-light.
why_now: Inventory near 88 days' supply and floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps tighten dealer cash. Contracts in transit stretch a week or more. After Sky Auto Mall, lenders have less tolerance for late payoffs. Private credit is searching for short-duration, self-liquidating receivables at high gross yield. LLM document parsing plus listing signals make per-deal verification cheap enough to underwrite $150 fee deals, which was not economical with a human ops desk.
revenue_model: A fee of about 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the payoff per roughly 9-day bridge, which is about 25 percent annualized gross, plus a 10 to 20 percent referral share to the floorplan lender, capital from a credit fund at about SOFR plus 6, and the startup keeping servicing fees and a first-loss or excess-spread slice. Illustration (assumptions): a dealer bridging 15 deals a month at $22k averages about $100k outstanding and pays about $2.1k a month. 5,000 dealers at that size is roughly $500M outstanding, about $125M of gross yield and perhaps $50M to $60M net after capital cost and losses. A $99 to $199 per dealer per month clock subscription is the top-of-funnel product.
non_obvious_insight: The listing-disappearance signal is too noisy to accuse a dealer but precise enough to underwrite a nine-day secured advance, because a false positive costs a declined bridge and not a false fraud allegation. Paying the floorplan lender directly makes the lender's SOT exposure structurally zero for bridged deals, so the lender is a willing distributor and co-subsidizer, and no lender integration is needed at the start because the dealer supplies the payoff quote. Detection was always a workaround for a timing mismatch that capital can simply remove.
first_30_days: Ask two independent floorplan lenders to name their 10 dealers with the most aged, late payoffs for timing reasons and to introduce us. Draft a term sheet with one credit fund or family office for a $500k to $1M pilot facility. Engage commercial-finance counsel on state licensing (some states license commercial lending and receivables purchases). Build the dealer-side Unpaid VIN clock as a landing page plus a manual crawler for the pilot dealers' sites. Aim to sign LOIs with 5 dealers and one capital source, and run the first three concierge bridges by hand to measure dilution, decline and cycle time.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors puts capital at risk or takes payoff timing risk. Vero, Solifi, SBS, LotCount, CSI, Netresult, DRN and MOBI all police or monitor, and sell to lenders. This sells to dealers, pays lenders and shares economics with them, so it is complementary and creates no channel conflict. Audit vendors and platforms gain lower-loss books, and if lenders accept Day-Zero they need fewer audits, which is a threat to audit revenue but a benefit to lenders. NextGear and Cox is the real latent competitor because it owns floorplan plus Dealertrack contract flow, but it can serve only NextGear dealers, while independents will not send their dealers to a Cox product. The parent's research did not cover contract-in-transit funding or dealer factoring providers, so checking those incumbents is step zero. Regulatory and capital risks are the main reasons this is the highest-variance offspring.
